title: Chapter 89 — Service, Retention, and The Long Relationship
intro: The service partnership, retention saves, and the decade view that turns one-time buyers into lifetime customers.

sections.title: Service Is Selling
sections.content:
When a customer calls with a service issue — a delivery problem, a warranty question, a product concern — that is not an interruption. It is a selling opportunity.

How you handle the problem determines whether they come back. A customer whose problem is solved quickly and professionally becomes more loyal than a customer who never had a problem at all.

Service recovery is one of the most powerful relationship-building moments in retail. Do not avoid it. Embrace it.

sections.title: The Retention Save
sections.content:
Sometimes a customer wants to return a product. Before processing the return, ask what went wrong. Maybe the product is fine but was installed incorrectly. Maybe they need a feature they did not know the product had. Maybe they just need reassurance.

Not every return is a lost sale. Some are problems waiting to be solved. The salesperson who investigates before processing saves sales that others give away.

sections.title: The Decade View
sections.content:
Think in decades, not transactions. A customer you serve well today may buy from you seven or eight more times over the next twenty years. They may refer dozens of friends. Their children may become customers.

That is the real value of great service. Not the immediate problem solved — the relationship preserved. The decade view changes how you think about every interaction, every follow-up, and every service call.

Do not think of your customer list as a record of past sales. Think of it as a community of people who trusted you enough to make one of the largest purchases for their home. Protect those relationships.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating service and retention, ask:

Does the salesperson treat service calls as opportunities or interruptions?
Do they investigate returns before processing them?
Do they think in terms of decades and lifetime value — or just today's sale?
Are they building relationships that will generate business for years?

Retention is cheaper than acquisition. Always.
